lessons.title: Army Values in practice
lessons.summary: Use the Army Values to make a defensible choice when speed, loyalty, or social pressure pull in different directions.
objectives: Explain how duty, respect, integrity, and personal courage apply when a teammate asks you to overlook a discrepancy.
lessons.sourceLocator: Army Values, Loyalty, Duty, Respect, Integrity, and Personal Courage.

sections.heading: Values guide choices
sections.text: The seven Army Values are Loyalty, Duty, Respect, Selfless Service, Honor, Integrity, and Personal Courage. The labels overlap in practice. An accurate report can be an act of integrity, a way to fulfill a duty, and an example of the moral courage it takes to speak up under pressure. Name the behavior and the people it affects before assigning a value to it.

sections.heading: A discrepancy is information
sections.text: Suppose your teammate asks you to initial a check you did not observe so the group can finish on time. Record what was actually checked, tell the person responsible what remains open, and offer to help complete the check. Respect includes giving your teammate a chance to correct the mistake without humiliating them. Loyalty to the team includes protecting others from decisions based on a false record.

sections.heading: What makes a decision defensible
sections.text: A useful explanation connects the standard, the fact you observed, and the correction you proposed. When the right reporting channel is unclear, get clarification from the responsible leader instead of changing the facts or advertising an unverified accusation.

questions.prompt: A team is late. Someone asks you to mark an inspection complete before it happens. What should you record and why?
questions.answer: Record the incomplete status, notify the responsible leader, and help arrange the check. Integrity keeps the record accurate, and duty protects the people who rely on it.

questions.prompt: A teammate notices their own reporting error before anyone acts on it. How can you help them correct it while practicing respect?
questions.answer: State the specific discrepancy and the real status, help correct the record through the appropriate channel, and keep the discussion about the task. Respect protects dignity and supports accountability.

lessons.title: Read a task standard
lessons.summary: Translate an Army training requirement into a practice plan and a fair evaluation.
objectives: Distinguish a task's conditions, standard, and performance measures and use them to interpret an observed result.
lessons.sourceLocator: ADP 7-0, chapter 4, evaluation and assessment. CAR task 071-COM-1012, Conditions, Standards, and Evaluation Guidance.

sections.heading: Three things to read
sections.text: A task names the action. The conditions describe the circumstances and resources under which it is evaluated. The standard defines acceptable performance. Performance measures turn that standard into observable checks. Before practicing, ask what the evaluator must see and what equipment, help, or time the conditions permit.

sections.heading: Evidence before a rating
sections.text: A learner who can explain a task may still miss a required performance measure during an attempt. Record the missing measure and the context. If a station's setup gives the learner equipment unavailable under the stated conditions, describe that difference as well. Those observations are more useful for retraining than a global judgment about ability.

sections.heading: Worked evaluation record
sections.text: On the map-to-ground task, the assigned sheet and visible terrain belong to the conditions. Correctly orienting the map relative to that terrain is the outcome. The evaluator records whether the learner met each required measure. If the lane did not provide the required view, record that condition gap and repeat under a valid setup. Keep it separate from feedback on an action the learner actually missed.

sections.heading: Practice and evaluation
sections.text: Use the current task record and training and evaluation outline when one applies. Practice can isolate one weak step, then the unit can reassess the whole task under the required conditions. Record study activity and evaluated performance separately so leaders can tell which evidence they have.

questions.prompt: An evaluator provides an electronic aid that the specified conditions exclude. The learner reaches the right answer. What can you conclude?
questions.answer: The attempt may show useful practice, but it does not demonstrate performance under the required conditions. Record the difference and reevaluate with the prescribed setup.

questions.prompt: Two learners miss the same performance measure for different reasons. What should an evaluation record?
questions.answer: Record the observable measure and what each learner actually did under the task conditions. The different causes can then guide different practice.

lessons.title: Read the map margin
lessons.summary: Use map edition, legend, scale, and contour interval to decide what a map can tell you.
objectives: Interpret a map’s scale and contour interval and explain why the legend and edition matter.
lessons.sourceLocator: CAR task 071-COM-1000, 30 November 2022, pp. 2–4, colors, symbols, and marginal information. Range-control training map, scale and contour note.

sections.heading: Identify the sheet
sections.text: The margin identifies the map and explains how to interpret it. Check the sheet and edition before comparing two maps of the same place. The legend explains the symbols the mapmaker used. Even familiar colors can have a specific meaning on a particular product, so inspect the legend before using a symbol as evidence.

sections.heading: Find the part of the margin that answers the question
sections.text: Use the sheet name, number, series and edition to identify the product, and the adjoining-sheets diagram to find the next sheet. The grid notes explain how positions are labeled. Projection and horizontal datum describe how ground positions are represented. The vertical datum concerns elevation, and the contour note gives the interval. The declination diagram identifies north references. Matching contour intervals on two sheets does not mean that their horizontal references match.

sections.heading: Check the provenance and overview notes
sections.text: Map margins can also summarize the area and how the sheet was made. The elevation guide gives a broad overview of relief. The boundary index locates administrative areas, and the adjoining-sheets diagram shows map coverage instead. The control, preparation, and printing notes help explain the source and production history. A spheroid is the reference shape used in representing the earth’s surface. Check the sheet’s coordinate and production notes when combining products or when an old sheet disagrees with current ground observations.

sections.heading: Read horizontal and vertical information separately
sections.text: A scale of 1:50,000 means that one unit on the original map represents 50,000 of the same units on the ground. A contour interval is the elevation difference between adjacent regular contour lines. Closely spaced lines indicate a steeper slope than widely spaced lines when the scale and contour interval are the same.

sections.heading: Combine the legend, shape, and color
sections.text: The CAR report groups common conventions such as black for many built features and labels, blue for water, and green for selected vegetation. Older and red-light-readable products can use brown, red, or red-brown differently. Treat color as a clue. Confirm the symbol’s shape and the sheet’s legend before calling a blue area a pond, marsh, or another water-related feature.

sections.heading: Know when the display changed
sections.text: Print scaling or zooming a screenshot can change the size of the map on paper or screen. Check a scale bar that was resized with the image, or use an original-size map for ruler measurements from its printed ratio. When terrain and map disagree, keep the discrepancy visible instead of treating an approximate match as certainty.

sections.heading: Worked scale check
sections.text: On an original-size 1:50,000 sheet, 3.2 centimeters represents 160,000 centimeters, or 1.6 kilometers of horizontal map distance. That is a straight-line measurement between the two marks. The contour note gives a separate vertical interval. On a resized copy, use the bar scale reproduced with that copy.

questions.prompt: A 1:50,000 map was shrunk to fit a printer page. What should you check before converting a ruler measurement?
questions.answer: Use a scale bar that shrank with the map, or an original-size copy with the printed ratio. The original ratio no longer describes the resized print at its physical size.

questions.prompt: On one map, two slopes cross the same number of regular contour intervals. One has lines much closer together. What changes?
questions.answer: Both slopes span the same elevation change. The closer contours span less horizontal distance, so that slope is steeper.

questions.prompt: A feature continues beyond the edge of a map. A second sheet has the same contour interval but a different edition. Which information helps you choose the neighboring sheet and use it alongside the first?
questions.answer: Use the adjoining-sheets diagram and sheet identifiers to select the neighbor. Check the edition, grid notes and horizontal reference before comparing positions. The shared contour interval describes elevation spacing on each sheet.

questions.prompt: A blue symbol looks similar to one you remember as a pond. Its outline and hatching differ. What evidence should settle the interpretation?
questions.answer: Use the legend for the specific sheet. Blue suggests a water-related feature, while the symbol’s shape and hatching distinguish what kind of feature it is.

lessons.title: Terrain association and uncertainty
lessons.summary: Compare identifiable ground features with the map before deciding that you have a match.
objectives: Explain why independently matching multiple terrain features supports map orientation better than a single similar feature.
lessons.sourceLocator: CAR task 071-COM-1012, purpose and task standard. Army NCO Academy coverage of supervised map reading and land navigation.

sections.heading: Compare relationships
sections.text: Terrain association uses recognizable features and how they relate to one another. A hill alone can look like many hills. A hill beside a bend in a road with a valley on one side gives several clues. A convincing match explains the shape, relative position, and orientation of the visible features together.

sections.heading: Treat uncertainty as evidence
sections.text: When one prominent feature fits but the surrounding pattern does not, there may be more than one plausible location or the sheet may be out of date. Keep alternate matches open and explain which feature conflicts with your first interpretation. This reasoning is useful at a training station because the instructor can check how you reached your answer.

sections.heading: Move the skill to a supervised lane
sections.text: An on-screen map exercise lets you practice interpreting evidence. The field standard requires the learner to relate a map to the actual ground under the task conditions. Practice that with the current training materials, the designated area, and the instructor’s safety and evaluation rules.

questions.prompt: A ridge fits the map, but the valley is on the opposite side from where you expect it. What does that tell you?
questions.answer: The ridge alone is weak evidence. Check the orientation and other independent features before committing to the interpretation. Report the disagreement if it remains unresolved.

questions.prompt: A learner correctly compares two diagrams on a screen. What evidence is still needed for the map-to-ground task?
questions.answer: An observed attempt in the field under the current task conditions. The screen exercise demonstrates conceptual reasoning and does not supply the conditions for the field performance.

lessons.title: Platoon, squad, and team responsibilities
lessons.summary: Understand the roles in the infantry example and how responsibilities fit together during ordinary training.
objectives: Distinguish the platoon leader, platoon sergeant, squad leader, and team leader in an infantry platoon example.
Compare headquarters and rifle squad responsibilities.
lessons.sourceLocator: ATP 3-21.8, chapter 1, section II, Duties and Responsibilities, pp. 1-7–1-12.

sections.heading: Read the organization as a set of responsibilities
sections.text: In the infantry example, the platoon leader is responsible for what the platoon does or fails to do. The platoon sergeant is the senior NCO, advises the platoon leader, and has important readiness and sustainment responsibilities. Their duties complement one another. Delegating an action does not erase the leader’s responsibility for the outcome.

sections.heading: Move up and down a level
sections.text: The squad leader is accountable for the squad and directs its teams. Team leaders supervise their Soldiers and communicate the team’s status through the squad leader. An issue that fits the team’s authority can be corrected at that level. A shortfall that affects multiple groups needs to reach the leader who can reallocate resources or change the plan.

sections.heading: Headquarters responsibilities and squad responsibilities
sections.text: The platoon headquarters combines information from squads and coordinates platoon-wide decisions and support. In the infantry example the platoon leader owns the overall task, the platoon sergeant helps maintain readiness and coordinates support, and the radiotelephone operator supports headquarters communication. A rifle squad turns its assignment into work for its teams, checks progress, and reports conditions that may affect the larger platoon. A team reports an actual count or result through its squad. The headquarters can use reports from several squads to make a resource decision. The person carrying the report does not thereby own the decision.

sections.heading: Use the example with care
sections.text: The publication describes an infantry rifle formation. Other formations and temporary teams can use different positions and reporting paths. Before a training event, confirm who assigned your task, who can change it, and who must know when the status changes.

questions.prompt: Two teams need the same limited training equipment. Which decisions belong at team level, and which need the squad or platoon?
questions.answer: Team leaders verify holdings and requirements and report the shortfall. The squad leader can resolve a squad-level allocation, while a platoon-level shortfall goes to the responsible platoon leaders.

questions.prompt: Why should a platoon leader still know about a supply issue the platoon sergeant is handling?
questions.answer: The platoon sergeant can coordinate sustainment, while the platoon leader needs its effect on readiness and owns decisions about the platoon’s activity.

questions.prompt: During a supervised training event, two squads report missing equipment, and one spare kit is available at headquarters. What information should the teams provide, and who owns the larger allocation decision?
questions.answer: The teams verify and report what is missing, who is affected and when the items are needed through their squad leaders. Headquarters combines the reports. The platoon leader owns the platoon-wide decision, the platoon sergeant coordinates support, and a communicator can relay the decision without making it.

lessons.title: Pass information that can be acted on
lessons.summary: Turn an observation into a clear status update and confirm that responsibility transferred.
objectives: Give an unambiguous training handoff that identifies the observed condition, its impact, and the next owner.
lessons.sourceLocator: ATP 3-21.8, chapter 1, section II, Exercise of Command and Control. ADP 7-0, chapter 4, preparation, execution, and assessment.

sections.heading: Separate observation and conclusion
sections.text: Distinguish what you checked from what you inferred. 'Two kits remain unchecked' describes evidence. 'All kits are ready' draws an unsupported conclusion from it. Good reporting gives the recipient enough context to make a decision and clearly identifies what remains uncertain.

sections.heading: Name the next owner
sections.text: At a training handover, state what is complete, the open item, why it matters, and who has the next action. When a detail affects someone else's work, ask the receiving person to confirm the action or repeat the critical information. Sending a message and transferring responsibility are two different events.

sections.heading: Update when the situation changes
sections.text: A status becomes stale when the underlying condition changes or the recipient misses the original message. Time-stamp important observations in the unit’s usual format, correct mistakes promptly, and use the established reporting channel instead of assuming everyone saw the same message.

questions.prompt: A relief team hears 'equipment is good' but two kits were never checked. What should the handoff say?
questions.answer: Name the two unchecked kits, identify what was actually verified, explain whether the gap affects the next event, and confirm who will complete the checks.

questions.prompt: You sent a message naming a next action, but nobody acknowledges taking it. What remains unresolved?
questions.answer: Ownership remains unresolved. Confirm the recipient and the next action through the designated channel before treating the handoff as complete.

lessons.title: Rehearse a training event
lessons.summary: Use a rehearsal to find gaps in roles, resources, and safety arrangements before execution.
objectives: Explain what a supervised training rehearsal should test and how to handle a discovered gap.
lessons.sourceLocator: ADP 7-0, chapter 4, planning and preparation. Army Training Management Directorate, TC 7-0.3 Plan an Event and TC 7-0.4 Training and Evaluation Outlines.

sections.heading: Make the sequence visible
sections.text: A rehearsal lets participants see how their responsibilities connect. In a classroom-to-field training event, walk through where the learner reports, who sets up each station, who evaluates the standard, and who can pause the event. Ask the people doing the work to explain when they act and what they need from the preceding group.

sections.heading: Turn gaps into changes
sections.text: A missing evaluator, a duplicated booking, or unclear safety authority is a planning fact. Identify an owner and a decision deadline, tell affected teams, and confirm the revision. If a required safety control is unresolved, bring the issue to the designated authority before execution.

sections.heading: Rehearsal and evaluation have different jobs
sections.text: A rehearsal can reveal that the plan is unclear. An evaluation checks actual performance against the training standard. A smooth rehearsal without the right conditions or equipment does not substitute for evaluation.

questions.prompt: At the rehearsal, both station leaders expect someone else to perform the equipment check. What should happen before execution?
questions.answer: Assign one owner, confirm the condition and timing of the check, and make the change visible to both stations and the event lead.

questions.prompt: Could a smooth rehearsal establish that every participant met the task standard?
questions.answer: Only if the attempt was actually evaluated under the applicable conditions and standard. Otherwise the rehearsal shows that participants practiced the sequence.

lessons.title: After-action reviews that improve training
lessons.summary: Turn a shared observation into one practical change the team can test.
objectives: Use evidence from a training event to identify a sustain, an improve, and a specific next action.
lessons.sourceLocator: Training Management Directorate, TC 7-0.1 description. ADP 7-0, chapter 4, evaluation and assessment.

sections.heading: Anchor the discussion
sections.text: An after-action review works from the intended task or standard and what participants observed. Ask what the group expected, what happened, and which conditions explain the difference. Surface observations from people at different stations rather than assuming the leader saw the whole event.

sections.heading: Separate sustain from improve
sections.text: Keep what worked and name the evidence supporting it. Describe a shortfall precisely enough to change one behavior. 'Handoffs were bad' is difficult to act on. 'Two of three shifts received no status on open equipment checks' identifies a gap worth addressing.

sections.heading: Test the explanation against the event
sections.text: If a group missed a start time, first compare the published schedule, the announcement each group received and the observations from the stations. An old board suggests a version problem. A current board that nobody could check suggests an access or handoff problem. Try a fix that addresses the observed cause and decide how the next group will check the result. Record an open question if the evidence is mixed.

sections.heading: Close the loop
sections.text: Pick a change, an owner, and a chance to test it at the next event. Use the next evaluation to see whether the change worked. This keeps the AAR connected to the training cycle and gives the team a chance to sustain a real improvement.

questions.prompt: An AAR finds that two shift changes left work unassigned. Give one concrete improvement and a way to test it.
questions.answer: Assign the outgoing lead to name an owner for each open item and obtain acknowledgement. At the next event, sample handoffs and check whether every open item has a confirmed owner.

questions.prompt: A leader remembers a clear briefing, but three participants report different start times. How should the AAR handle the difference?
questions.answer: Compare the intended time, what each group received, and which version was available at the point of action. Use those observations to improve how the schedule is confirmed.

questions.prompt: Two stations started late. One followed an old printed schedule. The other had the current schedule but no one acknowledged it at shift change. What should the AAR record and how could the team test the fixes?
questions.answer: Record the different causes and the observations supporting them. Remove obsolete schedules for the version problem and add acknowledgement at the handoff for the second. At the next event, check both the version in use and whether the receiving lead acknowledged it.

lessons.title: Who keeps a field site healthy?
lessons.summary: Distinguish the Soldier’s daily responsibilities from the unit field sanitation team’s role and command decisions.
objectives: Explain who observes, reports, advises, and owns corrective action when a field health control fails.
Match basic pest-prevention measures to an exposure pathway and the person responsible.
lessons.sourceLocator: ATP 4-25.12, chapters 1–2, Unit Field Sanitation Teams and Soldier Responsibilities, and chapter 6, Pest Management, sanitation and physical control.

sections.heading: A shared system
sections.text: The unit field sanitation team helps leaders identify and control preventable health threats. It contributes observation, checks, education, and advice. Leaders establish and enforce controls. Individual Soldiers make those controls work every day when they follow approved water and food practices, keep shared areas clean, and report deficiencies.

sections.heading: Look for failures in controls
sections.text: Work backward from a possible exposure. An empty handwashing point affects everyone using the dining area. A leaking waste container can contaminate surfaces and attract pests. Identifying the failed control helps leadership contain the problem, assign an owner, and determine whether preventive medicine or another specialist needs to assess it.

sections.heading: Report so someone can act
sections.text: Include the exact location, what changed, when you observed it, how it could affect others, and any immediate steps already taken under unit procedures. If you do not know what caused it, say so. Follow up to see whether the control was restored.

sections.heading: Choose controls that match the exposure
sections.text: Uncovered refuse or food residue can give flies and rodents food or shelter near a serving area. Restore basic site controls through the designated process: use covered collection, clean affected areas, and report what remains. Arthropod exposure during outdoor work calls for the personal protective measures assigned for that activity. Cleaning a food area and using personal barriers address different pathways.

sections.heading: Separate personal prevention from specialist work
sections.text: Soldiers use assigned precautions and report bites, visible pest activity, or failed controls through the normal unit process. Leaders keep shared sanitation controls working. The field sanitation team checks conditions and advises leaders when the problem requires preventive medicine or specialist support. A pest sighting alone does not justify selecting or applying a pesticide.

questions.prompt: A handwashing point outside a serving area is empty. Who can contribute to fixing the problem?
questions.answer: The observer reports the location and status. The responsible unit personnel restore the supply, the field sanitation team helps assess the control, and leaders make and enforce any decision about continued service.

questions.prompt: What makes 'the camp is unsanitary' less useful than a report about a specific broken control?
questions.answer: It does not say where the failure is, who is exposed, or what needs to change. Reporting the observed condition and its location gives leaders a corrective action they can assign and check.

questions.prompt: One team reports flies around an uncovered serving-area waste bin. Another reports ticks after outdoor work. Which controls apply to each report?
questions.answer: Restore covered collection and food-area sanitation controls for the fly problem. Follow the assigned personal protective measures for tick exposure and report it as directed. Give the field sanitation team the locations and observed failures so it can advise on further support.

lessons.title: Potable water from source to cup
lessons.summary: Understand how an approved water supply can become unsafe after it leaves its source.
objectives: Distinguish potable from palatable water and identify failures in the approval, storage, and dispensing chain.
lessons.sourceLocator: ATP 4-25.12, chapter 3, paragraphs 3-7 and 3-22–3-23, and section VII on water storage equipment.

sections.heading: Approval is evidence
sections.text: Potable water meets the applicable drinking-water requirements. Palatable water looks, smells, or tastes acceptable. A clear container proves little about potability, and an unpleasant taste alone does not establish the water’s status. Use the approved water supply and the unit’s designation for drinking, cooking, and other uses that require it.

sections.heading: Protect the chain after treatment
sections.text: The supply passes through containers, hoses, fittings, and taps before it reaches each person. A dirty fitting or a container previously used for something else can defeat the upstream controls. Keep potable and nonpotable equipment identified and separate, and report compromised seals, unclear labels, or unverified transfers.

sections.heading: Escalate uncertainty
sections.text: If a container’s status is unknown, report it and use a verified supply while the responsible personnel establish its status under unit procedures. Field sanitation checks and preventive medicine oversight belong in the approval process. Appearance or an improvised test cannot substitute for that process.

questions.prompt: Two similar containers sit beside the approved water point. One has no label and nobody can confirm its source. Which supply should you use?
questions.answer: Use the verified supply. Report the unidentified container and keep it out of drinking-water use until responsible personnel establish its status.

questions.prompt: Water came from an approved supply but passed through a hose of unknown use. Why does the original approval fail to settle the question?
questions.answer: Contamination can be introduced during transport or dispensing. Verify the equipment and report the questionable transfer under unit procedures.

lessons.title: Break the food and waste exposure chain
lessons.summary: Connect hygiene, clean equipment, protected food, and controlled waste disposal.
objectives: Identify where contamination could move between people, food, equipment, and waste.
lessons.sourceLocator: ATP 4-25.12, chapter 4, sanitary food handling and food-handler hygiene. Chapter 5, waste classification and management.

sections.heading: Follow contact, not appearances
sections.text: Food can be exposed by dirty hands, utensils, surfaces, or storage conditions even when a serving area looks orderly. Trace what each implement touched. Separate contaminated equipment and waste handling from clean food-service work, and follow the designated hygiene and sanitation controls before returning to service.

sections.heading: Keep waste streams distinct
sections.text: Waste comes in different forms and needs different handling. A full waste receptacle, a leak, or a disposal point that interferes with food or water operations deserves a specific report. Follow unit collection and disposal arrangements. Changing the site or handling method can create another exposure pathway.

sections.heading: Contain and communicate
sections.text: If a possible breach affects service, tell the responsible person what was exposed, how, and for how long if known. Hold affected items for the responsible decision under local procedures. A timely, accurate report can prevent more people from sharing the exposure and help identify which other items need review.

questions.prompt: A server handles refuse and returns to a serving table wearing the same gloves. What is the control failure?
questions.answer: The gloves can carry contamination from refuse to food or serving equipment. Stop the cross-contact, follow the required hand hygiene and clean-equipment controls, and report any possible exposure.

questions.prompt: A waste container leaks on a path used to deliver clean supplies. Is replacing the container the only issue?
questions.answer: No. The leaked material may contaminate the path, equipment, or deliveries. Report the location and path of exposure so responsible personnel can restore controls and address the affected area.

lessons.title: Heat and cold are exposure problems
lessons.summary: Understand why environmental risk changes with the task, clothing, and conditions.
objectives: Recognize changing exposure and identify unit prevention and escalation responsibilities.
lessons.sourceLocator: ATP 4-25.12, chapters 7–8, heat risk factors, prevention tools, and cold injury factors.

sections.heading: Consider the person, the task, and the environment
sections.text: Heat risk changes with effort, heat exposure, acclimatization, and clothing or equipment that limits heat loss. A familiar air-temperature reading does not by itself describe risk during hard work. Leaders use applicable heat monitoring and unit guidance to adapt workload, rest, and access to approved drinking water.

sections.heading: Cold exposure can persist above freezing
sections.text: Wet clothing, wind, long stationary periods, and contact with cold surfaces all affect heat loss. Weather alone does not show a Soldier’s exposure. Plan for dry clothing and shelter as directed and recheck conditions after a shift, rest period, or equipment change.

sections.heading: Report changes early
sections.text: Tell the responsible leader when a control is missing or exposure has changed. Promptly alert qualified help for a person whose condition is worsening, especially changes in responsiveness. Describe what changed and when. Symptom recognition and reporting support qualified assessment.

questions.prompt: The air temperature is unchanged, but a low-effort task becomes strenuous while the group is wearing more protective clothing. What should be reconsidered?
questions.answer: Reassess exposure and the unit’s prevention controls. Higher effort and more restrictive clothing can increase heat stress even at the same air temperature.

questions.prompt: A team is stationary in wind and rain at a temperature above freezing. Why should conditions be reassessed?
questions.answer: Wet clothing, wind, and inactivity can increase heat loss above freezing. Check whether existing clothing, shelter and monitoring controls are sufficient under unit guidance.

lessons.title: First-responder roles and TCCC phases
lessons.summary: Learn what role-based training and the phases of care tell a nonmedical Soldier about responsibilities.
objectives: Distinguish the All Service Members tier from higher tiers and explain why TCCC phases depend on context.
lessons.sourceLocator: ATP 4-02.11, chapter 3, pp. 27–35. JTS role-based education and training tiers, and current TCCC Guidelines, phase headings.

sections.heading: Tier answers who is trained for what
sections.text: TCCC stands for Tactical Combat Casualty Care. All Service Members training is Tier 1. Combat Lifesaver and medical personnel receive training for different roles. A technique appearing in the complete guideline may belong to a higher tier. Current role-based instruction and local direction are the references for what you are trained and expected to do.

sections.heading: Phase answers what context applies
sections.text: Care under fire or threat, tactical field care, and tactical evacuation care describe different circumstances involving safety, personnel, and available resources. The phase names help responders understand a handoff. They do not turn an urgent and changing situation into a fixed series of timed steps.

sections.heading: Apply tier and phase as separate checks
sections.text: A change in the setting can change what the next team can assess or support. It does not change an individual’s training tier. The JTS-listed May 2026 guidelines point to a separate en route care resource for detailed tactical evacuation guidance. Use phase names to follow the transition and role-based materials for the responsibilities you practice.

sections.heading: Use the correct training source
sections.text: ATP 4-02.11 replaced the older Army first-aid circular. The Army publication and current JTS materials serve complementary purposes: one provides Army doctrine, and the other tracks current role-based TCCC guidance and education. Use your approved training program for practice and evaluation.

questions.prompt: You find a technique in a provider-level guideline while studying Tier 1. Does its presence in the guideline establish that it is a Tier 1 skill?
questions.answer: No. Match the technique to the current All Service Members skill set and your approved training. The complete guideline addresses multiple roles.

questions.prompt: What information does a phase label carry when a casualty is handed to an evacuation team?
questions.answer: It gives context about the setting and available people or resources. The receiving team still needs the casualty’s current status and what has already happened.

lessons.title: Recognize and report urgent changes
lessons.summary: Practice the language of observation for time-sensitive problems so trained help receives a useful report.
objectives: Identify observations that warrant prompt escalation and report them without making an unsupported diagnosis.
lessons.sourceLocator: ATP 4-02.11, chapter 4 Overview of Massive Bleeding Control and chapter 5 Overview of Airway Control. JTS current guidelines, Tactical Field Care communications.

sections.heading: Describe what you can observe
sections.text: Severe ongoing bleeding, trouble breathing, or declining responsiveness are critical observations to communicate promptly through the designated response channel. Use plain language and a time reference where possible. A reported change such as 'was answering questions and now does not respond to voice' gives trained personnel better information than an unconfirmed diagnosis.

sections.heading: A clear report gives a trend
sections.text: A visible wound and changes in breathing or responsiveness convey different information. Give urgent changes promptly and include the earlier observation if known. For example, “At 1410 they answered normally. At 1415 they were harder to understand and appeared to be breathing with more effort.” State which findings you saw and which were reported by another person. An earlier reassuring observation does not cancel a later change.

sections.heading: Separate what happened from what you inferred
sections.text: State the known event, where the casualty is, what you saw, and what has changed. Say when the mechanism or a prior action is unknown. Clear uncertainty allows the person taking over to reassess. Passing along a guess as fact makes the next assessment harder.

sections.heading: Report a serious change when its cause is unclear
sections.text: Ongoing severe visible bleeding is an urgent observation. Changes in breathing or responsiveness also warrant prompt reporting when little blood is visible or you do not know the cause. The next responder needs the observations and timing to assess the casualty. Stay within your assigned role and use supervised Tier 1 training to practice the applicable assessment and care skills.

sections.heading: Apply the boundary in a scenario
sections.text: A practice question can teach which facts belong in a report and why a change is urgent. Hands-on training is where Soldiers learn to recognize conditions under pressure and demonstrate approved interventions under instruction. This lesson covers recognition and communication.

questions.prompt: A casualty who was speaking now struggles to answer and appears to have more difficulty breathing. What belongs in an immediate update?
questions.answer: Report the location, what changed in breathing and responsiveness, and when the change was observed. Request trained help through the designated channel and distinguish your observations from an unconfirmed cause.

questions.prompt: You did not witness the injury. Another person offers a guess about the cause. How should the cause be handed off?
questions.answer: Say that you did not observe the mechanism. Clearly label any secondhand account and pass along the signs, symptoms, times, and actions you actually know.

questions.prompt: During a supervised exercise, the first report mentioned a visible injury and normal speech. Five minutes later, the casualty is harder to understand and seems to be breathing with more effort. What should you send now?
questions.answer: Send an immediate update with location, the new breathing and responsiveness observations, and the time and earlier baseline if known. Request trained help through the designated channel and identify anything you did not observe. The earlier report does not represent the current condition.

lessons.title: Document and hand off with MIST
lessons.summary: Use the DD Form 1380 structure to preserve time, observations, and care information.
objectives: Distinguish the four MIST categories and explain how a written record complements a verbal handoff.
Identify which events and times the casualty card records and what must accompany the casualty.
lessons.sourceLocator: DD Form 1380 instructions, July 2025 update dated 21 July 2025, pp. 1–3 and Tables 1–2. JTS TCCC Guidelines, communications and documentation of care.

sections.heading: Put information where it helps the next responder
sections.text: MIST groups mechanism of injury, injuries, signs and symptoms, and treatments. Mechanism describes what happened. Injuries describe known injury locations or types. Signs and symptoms describe what responders observe or the casualty reports. Treatments record care already provided, with times when known.

sections.heading: A record travels between people and settings
sections.text: DD Form 1380 is the TCCC Casualty Card for point-of-injury documentation. It helps the next team understand care already provided when the original responder is unavailable. A verbal update can emphasize what has changed and answer questions. The written record preserves details across subsequent handoffs.

sections.heading: Read both sides and keep time references clear
sections.text: The front identifies the injury event and injury sites and has fields for information such as the type and application time of a previously applied tourniquet. It distinguishes the time of injury from later observations and care. For injury time, the instructions specify 24-hour notation with L for local or Z for Zulu. The reverse records treatment details and additional information such as notes and who provided the care. Read the field label before assigning a time to an event.

sections.heading: Keep unknowns visible
sections.text: Be precise about whether a time is observed, approximate, or unknown. Update the receiving team when the situation changes, and handle identifying information through approved channels. Use invented details in training exercises. These questions assess how information is grouped and communicated.

sections.heading: Follow the record to the receiving team
sections.text: The instructions say the completed card travels visibly attached to the casualty. Use the verbal handoff to draw attention to changes and explain unknown entries. If a note says “1400” without a reference or event, clarify whether it means injury, observation, or care and whether it is local or Zulu. If nobody can confirm it, pass the uncertainty forward.

questions.prompt: A fall was witnessed. The casualty reports pain, a responder notes a visible injury, and a trained responder reports care with a time. Where does each detail belong?
questions.answer: The fall is mechanism, the visible injury is injuries, reported pain is signs and symptoms, and care plus its time is treatments.

questions.prompt: A treatment is recorded on the card but its time is unknown. What should the next team hear?
questions.answer: Report the documented treatment and explicitly say the time is unknown. If appropriate, tell the team who provided the information so it can be verified.

questions.prompt: A practice casualty card records the fall at 1430Z. The outgoing responder says care was provided at 1500 but does not identify the time standard. Can you calculate the time from injury to care, and what should accompany the casualty?
questions.answer: A reliable elapsed time requires confirming the 1500 time standard. Keep 1430Z as the documented injury time, identify the uncertain time in the verbal handoff, and send the completed card with the casualty as the written continuity record.

lessons.title: Casualty movement and transfer of care
lessons.summary: Understand why moving a casualty and handing them off each require a coordinated training role.
objectives: Explain what continuity of care requires across a simulated casualty movement and transfer.
lessons.sourceLocator: ATP 4-02.11, chapters 1–2, casualty response terminology and casualty movement. DD Form 1380 instructions, background and policy.

sections.heading: Movement carries responsibilities
sections.text: Movement changes who can see the casualty, who can hear updates, and sometimes who is responsible for care. In a training scenario, know who is directing the move, who tracks the casualty’s status, and who is receiving them. Communicate a change in condition to the person responsible for care and confirm the receiving team has the record.

sections.heading: Keep the request and clinical handoff distinct
sections.text: An evacuation request coordinates movement and resources under a unit procedure. A clinical handoff communicates what the receiving team needs for continuity of care. Both can matter at the same time. Acknowledgment of a request does not establish that the receiving team has heard the casualty report or received the card.

sections.heading: Practice under an instructor
sections.text: Lifting, moving, and using a litter require hands-on practice with equipment and an instructor. Discuss the reporting responsibilities before the exercise, then demonstrate the assigned role under the task standard. The coverage map records movement as practical training.

questions.prompt: A simulated casualty has arrived at the receiving team, but the card stayed with the outgoing group. What part of the transfer is incomplete?
questions.answer: The continuity record has not transferred. Notify the receiving team, communicate what is known and unknown, and arrange transfer of the record through the approved process.

questions.prompt: An evacuation request is acknowledged. Why does the receiving team still need a separate status handoff?
questions.answer: The request coordinates movement. The handoff provides the casualty’s known mechanism, injuries, latest observations and care, including changes since the request.
